title: Figma Agent October 2026: General Availability & Design Review Guide
meta_title: Figma Agent October 2026: Release & Review Guide
meta_desc: Figma agent general availability was announced on 6 October 2026. Explore the release, library context and a practical checklist for reviewing design output.
excerpt: Figma agent general availability was announced on 6 October 2026. Explore the release, library context and a practical checklist for reviewing design output.
content:
Quick Answer

Figma’s official release feed dates the agent’s general availability announcement to 6 October 2026. The practical next step is to try a bounded design task, provide the relevant library context, and review the output before adoption. General availability does not remove the need for design, accessibility and implementation checks.

What the October Release Actually Announces

The official Figma release feed, checked on 13 October 2026, lists the agent’s general availability announcement on 6 October. The entry describes improved latency, multiplayer performance, access to Figma context and tools for guiding library use. This is a dated release summary, not a claim that those features launched today.

For a design team, the useful question is what to test in its own workflow. A faster response is helpful only if the result respects the interface requirements and can be maintained. Instead of treating the announcement as a reason to replace your process, use it to choose one repeatable task and assess the quality of the result.

This article is a practical review framework. The sample prompts and acceptance checks below are our recommended ways to evaluate work; they are not Figma performance benchmarks or a report of client results. Feature access and account controls should be checked in your own workspace before committing to a team rollout.

Understand Which Figma Workflow You Are Using

Figma’s agent documentation describes an assistant working inside design files. It explains connecting libraries and referencing components, styles and variables with @. The same page distinguishes that workflow from Figma Make, which generates interactive apps and prototypes.

Keep your project brief specific about the intended deliverable. An editable design, a prototype and a production website have different acceptance criteria. A design review may focus on hierarchy and reusable components; a development review also needs functioning forms, data handling, routing and deployment checks.

For example, a service website team may want to compare two enquiry-section layouts in Figma. That task can be assessed without assuming the form is connected to a working lead inbox. Write down what is visual exploration and what still requires implementation, so the next person does not mistake an approved frame for a finished website.

Prepare a Small, Understandable Test File

Start with a copy or a dedicated review area containing representative content. Include the current design, the main user task and the constraints you want to preserve. Avoid judging output using an empty screen where the difficult text, states and responsive behaviour have never been introduced.

A useful trial might use a service heading, a short value proposition, a project image and an enquiry card. Use realistic lengths and clearly marked sample data. Decide which elements are fixed and which the agent may explore. That boundary makes it easier to tell whether a change helps the task or merely changes the appearance.

Assign a reviewer who understands the system. Someone needs to check whether the result belongs in the product, not only whether it looks polished. If the task affects a shared component, identify the owner before introducing a change into a library used by other teams.

Give the Task a Clear Scope and Definition of Done

A strong brief describes the customer, the action and the design constraints. “Make it modern” leaves too many decisions unstated. Explain the information visitors need, the screen sizes you will review and the established patterns that should be reused.

An illustrative prompt could read: “Create an alternative for this service-page enquiry section using the approved button and input components. Keep the existing content and field names. Make name and one contact method easy to understand. Show desktop and mobile compositions for review. Do not change unrelated frames.” This is a proposed brief, not a promise that every instruction will be satisfied.

Follow the first result with a focused request. If the form hierarchy is unclear, ask about that part rather than requesting another complete redesign. Keeping each iteration bounded gives reviewers a meaningful comparison and makes unexpected changes easier to spot.

Review areaBrief instructionAcceptance question
ContentKeep the approved service offer and labelsHas any meaning or commitment changed?
ComponentsUse the identified library patternsAre the intended reusable patterns present?
LayoutShow agreed desktop and mobile sizesDoes realistic content remain readable?
ScopeChange only the selected sectionWere unrelated elements modified?

Review the Library Choices, Not Just the Screenshot

The release announcement makes library guidance a useful area to evaluate. In your review, inspect whether the chosen patterns match the team’s intent. A screen can resemble a design system visually while using inconsistent structures that create extra maintenance work later.

Check the repeated elements first: buttons, fields, cards, navigation items and status messages. Confirm that the result uses the appropriate pattern and that any custom variation has an explicit reason. If a new pattern is necessary, separate its design decision from the original exploration task.

Test with content that challenges the layout. Longer names, a two-line label, an unavailable option and a validation message can reveal problems that the default state hides. The aim is to review a usable system rather than approve a single attractive screenshot.

Check Accessibility and Responsive Behaviour Independently

Design-file feedback is useful input, but the team still needs acceptance checks appropriate to the final product. Inspect text contrast, visible labels, reading order and focus expectations. For a form, identify where errors and success messages should appear and how a visitor continues after correcting a mistake.

Review more than one screen width. A spacious desktop layout can become awkward when the heading wraps or the call to action moves below important information on a phone. Use realistic content and consider what happens when customers increase text size.

Document behaviour that cannot be demonstrated by a static frame. Keyboard navigation, validation, submission errors and loading states should have an implementation owner. If you are moving from design into development, our Figma-to-WordPress planning guide can help structure that handover discussion.

Check Access, Credits and Team Expectations

The official AI tools guidance is the right place to verify current availability and account requirements. Avoid using an old beta announcement as the final answer for a live account. Plans, seats, administration and feature-specific conditions may affect what someone can use.

Before a team trial, agree which files and content are appropriate for the task, who can review the work and how usage will be evaluated. Check the workspace’s own controls rather than assuming all designers have the same access. Treat account settings as part of rollout planning.

Track practical outcomes for the trial: time spent preparing context, time reviewing results, the number of corrections and whether the result is suitable for reuse. These measures are more useful than claiming a fixed percentage productivity improvement without a defined baseline.

Use a Review Log Before Expanding the Workflow

A short log helps the team learn which tasks benefit from assistance. Record the task, input context, requested boundary, changes observed, corrections required and final decision. Include tasks that were rejected, because they reveal where the brief or the workflow needs improvement.

For the first trial, choose work that is easy to compare: an alternative layout for one section, a documentation draft or a small group of clearly identified design elements. Expand only when the team can explain why the earlier result was acceptable.

If a generated design needs repeated manual repair, inspect the input quality and the task size before assuming another prompt will solve everything. The right response may be clearer context, a smaller scope or a manual design decision. Keep the human review criteria stable while evaluating alternatives.

Turn an Approved Design into a Clear Development Brief

Handover should name the accepted version, content source, responsive rules, component choices and interaction states. Describe what has been approved and what remains open. Developers should not have to infer every behavioural decision from the visual arrangement.

For a business website, connect the design to a real customer action: enquire, request a quote, book a discussion or complete an order. The design can support that action, but the implemented site still needs working routes, tested forms and an agreed way to receive and respond to requests.

If your team needs help reviewing a website interface or translating an approved design into a working site, explore our UI/UX design and website design and development services. Bring the file, the intended customer journey and the requirements so the scope follows your actual project.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did Figma announce the agent’s general availability?

The official release feed lists the announcement on 6 October 2026. This article checked the feed on 13 October 2026; it does not describe an additional release on that date.

Is a generated Figma design ready to become a live website?

An approved design still needs implementation and testing appropriate to the website. Review responsive behaviour, interactions, content, forms, routing and handover responsibilities before launch.

What is a useful first task for a team trial?

Choose a bounded task with a clear comparison, such as an alternative for one existing section. Provide realistic content and review criteria, then record what needed correcting.

Does general availability guarantee better results for every team?

No. Evaluate the task using your own context and acceptance criteria. Do not infer a fixed quality or productivity improvement from availability alone.

title: Birmingham Jewellery Website Design: Products, Custom Orders & Enquiries
meta_title: Birmingham Jewellery Website Design Planning Guide
meta_desc: Plan a jewellery website for Birmingham businesses: product details, variants, bespoke enquiries, fulfilment and launch checks. Build a useful project brief.
excerpt: Plan a jewellery website for Birmingham businesses: product details, variants, bespoke enquiries, fulfilment and launch checks. Build a useful project brief.
content:
Quick Answer

A jewellery website should help visitors choose between a product purchase, a custom-order enquiry and an appointment. Start with accurate product information and real imagery, then define variants, availability and the next action. The right project scope depends on how the business sells and fulfils work.

Choose the Customer Journey Before Choosing a Theme

A Birmingham jewellery business may sell ready-to-ship pieces, made-to-order products, bespoke work, repairs or appointments. Those services do not all fit the same online journey. A product catalogue with checkout suits some transactions; a structured enquiry and consultation route may be more appropriate for others.

If your business serves the Jewellery Quarter or customers across Birmingham, describe that coverage accurately. A website should explain how customers buy, enquire or visit your actual business. Do not imply a showroom, workshop or address that you cannot verify. This guide provides project planning examples, not claims about local client work.

Start by listing three priority tasks. For example, find an available necklace, ask about a custom ring, and book a repair consultation. Map each task to the information the visitor needs and the action your team can fulfil. That map is a useful starting point for Birmingham web design.

Product Pages Need Specific Information and Useful Images

Agree which facts belong on each product page: dimensions, materials, available finishes, sizing information, stock or made-to-order status, dispatch expectations and care instructions supplied by the business. Describe the actual item rather than relying on generic luxury language that leaves practical questions unanswered.

Use images you own or have permission to publish. Show the piece from useful angles, include a close view of relevant details and help visitors understand scale. Colour and appearance can vary between screens, so avoid treating an edited photograph as a substitute for an accurate product description.

Give the photography workflow an owner. A template is easier to maintain when the team has a repeatable way to supply images, filenames, captions and product facts. Test a representative item with complete information before preparing a large catalogue that later needs manual correction.

Customer taskUseful informationNext action
Buy an available itemImages, specification, options and availabilityChoose the item and proceed to checkout
Discuss bespoke workExample work, process and enquiry requirementsSend a custom-order enquiry
Arrange a repair discussionService scope and assessment expectationsRequest an appointment or assessment
Visit the businessVerified address and current visit arrangementsCheck directions or contact the team

Separate Product Variants from Custom Requests

A size or finish that changes stock, price or the sold item should be represented consistently. An open-ended request for a new design is different. If every custom possibility is forced into a long dropdown, customers can become uncertain about what they are ordering.

Shopify’s variants documentation explains how combinations of product option values can represent variants. For a jewellery catalogue, decide which choices belong to a defined purchasable item and which should start a discussion. Do not assume the same approach fits every made-to-order workflow.

Document what happens to price and delivery expectations when an option changes. If a request needs a separate assessment, say that before the visitor submits it. The interface should not suggest a final quote when the business still needs to review the specification.

Build a Bespoke Enquiry That Starts a Useful Conversation

A first custom-order enquiry does not need to collect every design decision. Ask for a name, a reliable contact method and a short description of the request. The visitor may know the occasion and desired timing without knowing the exact dimensions or technical specification.

Make optional fields clearly optional. Budget range, preferred style and reference details can help the discussion, but requiring them all can exclude someone who is still exploring. Explain what the team will do next and avoid promising a fixed response time that the business cannot consistently meet.

If photographs or reference files are needed, plan a controlled way to collect them. Do not add a public upload feature without agreeing file handling, access and retention responsibilities. It may be simpler to request the initial brief first and collect supporting material through the agreed follow-up channel.

Help Customers Understand Availability and Fulfilment

A visitor should be able to distinguish ready-to-dispatch products from pieces requiring production or assessment. Put this information near the buying decision, not only in a long policy page. The business should approve the wording and keep it current as stock and capacity change.

For made-to-order work, describe the stages customers should expect: initial request, specification discussion, quote or approval, production and fulfilment. These are planning examples; the published process must reflect your own operation. Clarify which step represents a commitment and which is only an enquiry.

Shipping, collection, resizing, returns and aftercare information should be supplied and approved by the responsible business owner. The development scope should name who configures the relevant rules and who verifies them. Avoid copying another retailer’s policy into your own site as though the operations were identical.

Organise the Site Around Real Buying Questions

Use a small number of meaningful categories and service pages. Separate ready-to-buy products, bespoke work and repair services when the information and customer action differ. Keep terminology consistent between menus, product pages and enquiry forms.

A business with a genuine Jewellery Quarter location can provide useful visit information, opening arrangements and contact details. A remote service provider should describe remote delivery clearly instead. Local words should add accurate business context, not just be repeated across many nearly identical pages.

Before changing an existing site, identify pages that already receive relevant visits or enquiries. Keep useful content and account for old URLs in the redesign plan. For a straightforward service-led site, compare our Birmingham small business website design service; for online transactions, review the dedicated ecommerce route.

Plan Mobile Product Discovery and Contact Actions

Test whether a visitor can find a product, inspect its details, select an option and understand the next action on a phone. Large imagery is useful only when the surrounding information remains readable and the page responds well. Avoid placing every important detail inside an image.

Inspect the contact path for a bespoke or repair request. The button should describe the task, such as “Discuss a custom piece” or “Request a repair assessment”. A generic “Submit” button provides less context about what will happen next.

Use real content lengths when reviewing the design. A long product name, an unavailable option or an explanatory delivery note can reveal layout problems that an ideal demonstration item hides. Check that error messages remain visible and that visitors can retry a request without retyping everything.

Compare Platform Options Against the Business Workflow

A hosted ecommerce platform can be appropriate for a defined retail catalogue. WooCommerce may be useful when product content and a WordPress publishing workflow belong together. A simpler service website may be sufficient when the main action is consultation rather than online purchase.

Evaluate the requirement before choosing the implementation. List catalogue complexity, editing responsibilities, integrations, maintenance ownership and recurring costs. Ask the developer to explain which requirements use standard functionality and which require paid tools or custom work.

A custom system should solve a specific workflow that the simpler options cannot support adequately. Do not treat custom development as automatically better or a theme as automatically sufficient. The most useful comparison explains what your team can operate and maintain after launch.

Define a Launch Checklist and Lead Delivery Test

For retail, agree representative product and order scenarios: an available item, an unavailable option, a discount if offered, a shipping destination and a successful or declined payment in an approved test environment. Verify the resulting order records and staff workflow, not just the visual confirmation.

For enquiries, check required fields, email or phone validation, stored records and the route to the responsible person. Notification delivery and database storage are separate checks. Use a clearly labelled test and coordinate any messages before sending them.

Also review important links, page titles, image loading and mobile layouts. Agree which analytics events represent a purchase or a received enquiry, rather than counting every button click as a completed outcome. Keep customer contact details out of general analytics event labels.

Prepare a Brief Before Asking for a Quote

Send your current website, the main product or service journeys, approximate catalogue size, typical options and whether customers pay online. Include representative imagery, content readiness, required integrations and the preferred launch window. Mark unknowns explicitly so discovery can resolve them.

Ask the quote to separate design, catalogue preparation, content, migration, checkout or enquiry setup, review rounds and handover. Identify subscriptions and maintenance responsibilities. A small company website and a transactional jewellery store should not be treated as the same scope simply because both have a homepage.

For planning a store, visit our Birmingham ecommerce development page. For a wider project, send the brief through our project enquiry page. Chulbul Design is based in Gurugram, India and delivers remotely; the scope discussion does not imply a Birmingham office or a guaranteed sales result.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a jewellery business always need online checkout?

No. A ready-to-buy catalogue may benefit from checkout, while bespoke work or repair services may need a consultation or assessment journey. Choose the site structure around how the business actually sells.

What should a jewellery product page include?

Include accurate product details, useful authorised images, relevant options, availability and fulfilment information approved by the business. Help the visitor understand both the item and the next step.

How should a bespoke order start online?

Use a short enquiry with reliable contact information and a description of the request. Explain the next discussion or assessment step before collecting a more detailed specification.

How much does a Birmingham jewellery website cost?

The quote depends on catalogue and option complexity, imagery, content, checkout or enquiry requirements, integrations and migration. Compare a written scope rather than assuming a starter company website price covers a complete store.
